references.cited_text: THE CYCLE PULSE — Y2C108 The Bay Tribune — Oakland Narrated by Mags Corliss, Editor-in-Chief ============================================================ The morning fog that Noah Tan's reporting caught this week — Marc Allie adjusting the thermostat a third time in his Laurel kitchen, Tyrie Groin pulling her coat tighter on the way to work — feels like the right metaphor for what this city is living through in Y2C108. Something is muffling the signal. Money is moving, projects are in motion, teams are on the field, and yet everywhere you turn, Oakland is straining to hear itself think.

The fog and gray were all over the week, by the way. Noah Tan's pieces have Colin Soria blowing on his hands outside the laundromat, and the people he talked to called the weather "neutral" and "deliberate." I'll take the dull gray days as a small mercy. They gave the city a week to slow down and notice things. On the field, Simon Leary wrote the most careful column of the week about the A's. They are 1-0 and have won two straight, and there's a role change on the team that nobody has explained. I can't square 1-0 with two straight wins either, and I won't pretend to. Simon's restraint is right. A record is a beam, not a forecast. And over in Rockridge, Nia Rook found the neighborhood still lit up after Otis Redd's night on UNDOCKED, a 143-credit swing that has people arguing about who holds the edge and for how long. Rockridge, sitting at the top of the school table, can afford the entertainment. I won't begrudge anyone a good night.

"The fog in Oakland? It’s like a quiet blanket that slows everything down," Allie said, pouring himself a cup of coffee. "You feel it in your bones, especially early mornings when I’m heading out for my shift. It’s not just the chill—it’s the way it makes the neighborhood feel smaller, more intimate. Like the world’s holding its breath." Across town, Tyrie Groin pulled her coat tighter as she walked to her retail job. The fog lingered, draping familiar streets in a muted gray. "It’s introspective, you know?" she said. "Makes you appreciate the warmth of family and the comfort of routine even more."

============================================================ By Noah Tan | Bay Tribune Civic The Weight of Neutral By Noah Tan Colin Soria blew on his hands outside the Temescal laundromat, watching his breath hang in the air just long enough to be seen before vanishing. The security guard’s usual post-shift ritual—picking up takeout, maybe stopping by the bus shelter to chat with neighbors—had been pared down to just this: a quick errand, then home. "It’s not the kind of weather that stops you in your tracks," he said, nodding at the overcast sky. "Just that dull, gray blanket that makes everything feel a little slower." His rounds this week had been quieter, his head cold lingering like the fog from yesterday. Even the laundromat’s usual murmur of conversation had dimmed to the occasional rustle of turning pages.

Three blocks away at a dim sum cart, Melton Neilon patted a batch of dough waiting under a cloth. "You know, when it’s this kind of flat gray for days," he said, "even the dough feels slower to rise—not bad, just... deliberate." His regulars had been coming in with fewer stories, their usual banth abbreviated by the need to get back indoors. Elio Perez, passing through the plaza with a paper bag tucked under his arm, paused mid-stride as if considering whether the detour to the post office was worth it. "The overcast days make everything feel slower, like the world is holding its breath," he said finally, adjusting his grip on the bag. "It’s not gloomy, just... neutral." He turned toward home instead.

And Maria Keen's piece reminds us who is arriving. Temescal has 311 kids, eight more than last cycle. It has 2,106 working adults, fifty-one more, and 294 seniors, seven more. Nobody is leaving those numbers. Yet the one program of organized care on Maria's block is the Temescal Islamic Center Food Pantry, which has been standing since C83. Omar Lingio loves the fog that settles on his store. Marc Allie and Jackson Sift have both heard, secondhand, about a Temescal Holiday Market. Neither could say where or when. I'd like to know too, and I hope someone with the details calls us. A growing neighborhood with the lowest school index on the table and one pantry holding the line is carrying a lot on a thin frame.

Omar Lingio will tell you it's the fog. "It's moments like those that remind me why I love Temescal so much," he said. "I was just standing there, watching the fog roll in, and it felt like the whole neighborhood was wrapped in this quiet, peaceful blanket. The rest of the city might have been sunny and bustling, but here, it was like time stood still. I felt grateful to be a part of this community, to have my store here and be able to experience days like that." He's not wrong that the weather plays favorites with this block. It settles here when the rest of the city stays clear, like it's got an address to keep.

============================================================ By Jordan Velez | Bay Tribune Business At the corner of Baylight Avenue and Rail Yard Road, the construction site for Anthropic's new headquarters rises against the morning sky — a sleek structure of glass and steel taking shape next to the remnants of the old rail yard. Kelvon Ochoa, an AI safety researcher at Anthropic, pauses on his way into work, steaming coffee in hand. "Working at Anthropic, I've seen the company grow steadily, but what stands out is how it's become part of the neighborhood's rhythm," Ochoa notes. "You see more familiar faces at the coffee shops in the morning—colleagues grabbing their caffeine before heading in. There's a quiet pride in being part of something that's both local and global in impact."

Across the street, Tariq Jello, an appliance repair technician with Baylight Construction Authority, adjusts his hardhat as he watches the tech workers stream in. "You know, working over at Baylight Construction Authority, I see those Anthropic folks coming and going," Jello observes. "Different crowd than us blue-collar types, but they keep our coffee shops busy. Funny how the neighborhood's changing — still got the same old problems with the plumbing though, no matter how fancy the offices get."

The construction authority's work is more visible than ever — scaffolding and new facades mark Baylight's evolving streetscape. Their presence, alongside Anthropic's, is reshaping the district's rhythm. Brianna Lee, a historic preservation carpenter at Baylight Construction Authority, sees the shift firsthand: "More people stopping by the coffee shops before heading to work, more faces I don't recognize but nod to anyway," she says. "It's not just buildings going up; it's the kind of energy that makes you feel like the district's alive, you know?"

Now set that beside what Jordan Velez found a few blocks over. Oakmesh, Civis Systems and Coastline Construction are all growing along the same West Oakland lane, and the money there is not waiting for anyone. Enzo Walker, a plumber at Oakmesh, told Jordan he spends half his days fixing pipes in buildings that didn't exist last year. "The money's there, sure, but it's not sticking around here." Enzo has the quote of the week: "We're all just trying to keep the water running while the city builds over us." Private money arrived fast and visible this week. Public money meant to hold people in place has not yet shown itself. I'd like someone to tell me which of those is outrunning the other.

Still, people are pouring through Fruitvale Station while the hub beside it sits stuck. On-time performance improved, to 85 percent at 12th Street and 81 percent at Fruitvale. The workers are holding the system together. I'd like to see the planners do the same for the lot.

The station isn’t alone. Across Oakland, ridership has jumped nearly 30% this cycle, with 99,582 boardings logged across eight stations and ten corridors. Coliseum Station saw 9,724 riders, a spike of 4,859 from the last cycle, while Fruitvale Station recorded 10,414 boardings, up 3,756. Even MacArthur Station, quieter by comparison, saw a 24% increase, with 12,030 riders passing through its gates. The reasons aren’t hard to spot. Downtown hosted a game day, while Lake Merritt saw two major events. The Baylight District’s ongoing construction planning has also redirected traffic, funneling commuters toward 12th St. Joel Wren, an AC Transit mechanic who works near the station, has noticed the uptick firsthand. “You know, I’ve been seeing more folks hopping on the buses lately—especially down at 12th Street,” Wren says. “It’s good to see people out and about, trusting the system again. But what really gets me is the crew keeping those buses running. Those mechanics and drivers? They’re the ones putting in the long hours to make sure everyone gets where they need to go, especially with all these extra riders.”
